newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Occidental says Colombia security worsens.
newsitem.headline: Occidental says Colombia security worsens.

text.p: The head of Occidental Petroleum's Colombian subsidiary said the security situation in Colombia has hit a new low as leftist rebels demonstrate an unprecedented ability to attack at will, crippling oil facilities and killing workers.
"The guerrillas are getting closer all the time to our key installations, they're surrounding us," said Occidental of Colombia president Stephen Newton.
"We're very concerned about our people, our contractors and obviously about our installations," Newton added in an interview with El Tiempo, Colombia's leading daily.

To drive home his point, he said five Occidental contract workers had been killed in rebel attacks so far this year as opposed to 14 in all of 1996. He also said 21 rebel sabotage attacks had been perpetrated against the company's key Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline since the start of the year, compared to an annual average of 45 attacks in previous years.
"At this rate we're going to reach historic figures in terms of the number of attacks on our infrastructure," Newton said.
He said 10 percent of Occidental's operating costs in Colombia already went to security, not including a so-called "war tax" or $17 million payment to the military this year.
The payments are the highest Occidental makes for security anywhere in the world, but Newton said the security situation was deteriorating steadily nonetheless.

"Unfortunately, the guerrillas can chose when and where they're going to attack," Newton said, adding that the 290-strong police and military force assigned to guard Occidental's oil facilities and workers was insufficient given beefed up rebel activity across the country.
Antonio Urdinola, the head of the state oil company, Ecopetrol, conceded that Colombia's security situation had worsened in an interview with El Tiempo just last week.

He also warned that foreign investment in the oil sector could come to a standstill unless the government succeeds in addressing the mounting security concerns of multinationals like Occidental and British Petroleum Co Plc.
"Today, all investment in the oil sector depends on the government's commitment to increase security," Urdinola said.
